title: Incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles and sex linkage
blurb: Solve crosses that break simple dominance: blends, ABO blood types, polygenic traits and X-linked disorders such as hemophilia.
question: A mother with type A blood and a father with type B blood have a child with type O blood. Is that possible? And if a mother carries the allele for hemophilia, why are her sons at risk while her daughters are not affected?

teach.h: When one allele does not simply win
teach.body: Mendel's pea traits showed complete dominance, but many traits do not. Formal definitions: in incomplete dominance the heterozygote shows an intermediate (blended) phenotype; in codominance both alleles are fully expressed; multiple alleles means more than two alleles exist in the population; polygenic traits are controlled by many genes; sex-linked genes sit on a sex chromosome. Plain English: sometimes the alleles mix, sometimes both show, and sometimes your sex decides how many copies you have.

teach.caption: With incomplete dominance the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio, because every genotype looks different. Sickle cell trait is codominant at the molecular level.

head: Blood type
Possible genotypes
teach.caption: Three alleles (IA, IB, i). IA and IB are codominant with each other, and both are dominant to i.

teach.h: IAi x IBi: four blood types
teach.caption: Each type has a 1/4 chance. A type A parent and a type B parent CAN have a type O child if both carry i.

teach.body: X-linked genes sit on the X chromosome. Females (XX) have two copies, so a recessive allele can be masked; a heterozygous female is a carrier. Males (XY) have one X, so a single recessive allele shows: males are hemizygous. That is why X-linked recessive disorders (hemophilia A, red-green color blindness, Duchenne muscular dystrophy) are much more common in males. A father passes his X to every daughter and his Y to every son. Y-linked traits pass father to son.

teach.caption: 50% of sons affected, 50% of daughters carriers, no affected daughters.

rows.label: Why
values: Dad gives X to girls, Y to boys

head: Pattern
Examples
rows: Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, Tay-Sachs, PKU
Hemophilia A, red-green color blindness, Duchenne MD
Height, skin color, eye color shades
teach.caption: Polygenic traits show a continuous range. Environment (such as nutrition and height) can also shape a phenotype.

teach.h: Worked scenario: reading the Jackson pedigree
teach.body: Keisha, a nursing applicant, studies her family pedigree (squares = males, circles = females, shaded = affected, half-shaded or dot = carrier). Her unaffected parents have an affected son and an unaffected daughter, and the condition skipped her grandparents' generation. Two unaffected parents with an affected child means the allele is recessive and both parents carry it. If only males across several generations are affected, through carrier mothers, X-linked recessive is the likely pattern.

teach.text: Classic mix-ups: incomplete dominance BLENDS (pink), codominance shows BOTH (AB, roan). Type O is RECESSIVE (ii), so two type O parents can only have type O children. An affected father does NOT pass an X-linked disorder to his sons: they get his Y. His daughters all get his X and become carriers.

items: Incomplete dominance: blend; red x white snapdragon F2 = 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
Codominance: both expressed (AB blood, roan cattle).
ABO: IA and IB codominant, both dominant to i; O = ii; AB = IAIB.
Polygenic: many genes, continuous range (height, skin color).
X-linked recessive: more common in males; carrier mom gives 50% of sons the trait; affected dad's daughters are all carriers.

summary: You can now tell incomplete dominance from codominance, work out ABO blood types from genotypes, and recognize polygenic traits. You can also predict X-linked recessive outcomes for sons and daughters and use pedigree clues to identify recessive and X-linked patterns.

A.q: Red snapdragons crossed with white snapdragons produce offspring that are all pink. This is an example of:
A.why: The heterozygote shows an intermediate blend (pink) of the two parental phenotypes: incomplete dominance.

whyNot.0: Codominance would show BOTH colors fully, such as red and white patches, not a blend.
whyNot.2: Multiple alleles means more than two alleles in the population; this cross involves two.
whyNot.3: Polygenic traits come from many genes and show a continuous range, not three tidy classes.

A.q: Which blood type results from the genotype IBi?
A.why: IB is dominant to i, so IBi has type B blood.

whyNot.1: Type AB requires both IA and IB (IAIB).
whyNot.2: Type O requires two recessive i alleles (ii).
whyNot.3: Type A requires an IA allele, which IBi does not have.

A.q: Why are X-linked recessive disorders such as hemophilia A far more common in males?
options: Males inherit their X from their father
The Y chromosome carries the disease allele
Males have one X, so one allele shows
Males need two copies of the allele to show it
A.why: Males (XY) have a single X, so one recessive allele on it is expressed; there is no second X to mask it.

whyNot.0: Males receive their X from their mother; the father gives them his Y.
whyNot.1: X-linked genes are on the X chromosome, not the Y.
whyNot.3: Females need two copies; males need just one because they have one X.

B.q: A woman who is a carrier for hemophilia (XHXh) and a man without hemophilia (XHY) have a son. What is the probability that the son has hemophilia?
B.why: A son gets his Y from his father and one of his mother's two X chromosomes; half the time it is Xh, so 50%.

whyNot.0: 25% is the chance for ANY child (of all four boxes, one is XhY); among sons alone it is 50%.
whyNot.1: The son can inherit his mother's Xh, so the risk is not zero.
whyNot.2: The mother also carries a normal XH, which half of her sons receive.

B.q: A red bull crossed with a white cow produces roan calves with a mix of separate red hairs and white hairs. Which pattern does this show?
B.why: Both alleles are fully expressed side by side (red hairs AND white hairs): codominance.

whyNot.1: Incomplete dominance would give a blended color (each hair pinkish), not separate red and white hairs.
whyNot.2: Nothing here depends on the calf's sex.
whyNot.3: This is one gene with two alleles, not many genes adding up.

B.q: Human height varies continuously across a wide range rather than falling into a few distinct categories. This is best explained by:
B.why: Many genes each add a small effect, producing a continuous range: polygenic inheritance (with nutrition also playing a part).

whyNot.0: Codominance of two alleles gives a few distinct phenotypes, not a smooth range.
whyNot.1: X-linked traits differ mainly between the sexes and give distinct categories.
whyNot.3: Multiple alleles of one gene, as in ABO, still give a few distinct classes.

C.q: A woman with type A blood (IAi) and a man with type B blood (IBi) have a child. What is the probability that the child has type O blood?
C.why: Each parent can pass i. IAi x IBi gives IAIB, IAi, IBi and ii, so type O (ii) has a 1/4 chance.

whyNot.0: Type O is possible because both parents carry the recessive i allele.
whyNot.2: 1/2 would need two of the four boxes to be ii; only one is.
whyNot.3: 3/4 is the chance the child is NOT type O.

C.q: A man with red-green color blindness (XcY) and a woman homozygous for normal vision (XCXC) have children. Which outcome is expected?
options: All daughters carriers; no sons affected
Half of sons affected; daughters normal
Half of the daughters affected; sons normal
C.why: Every daughter gets the father's Xc plus a normal XC (carrier); every son gets his Y and a normal XC from his mother.

whyNot.1: Sons receive their father's Y, not his X, and their mother has only normal alleles.
whyNot.2: Sons get their X from the mother, who is XCXC, so none are affected.
whyNot.3: Daughters get one normal XC from their mother, so they are carriers, not affected.

C.q: Two parents without a disorder have a child who has it, and the disorder affects males and females equally in the family. Which inheritance pattern is most likely?
C.why: Unaffected parents with an affected child means both carry a hidden recessive allele; equal effects in both sexes point to an autosome.

whyNot.1: A dominant disorder would show in at least one parent of an affected child.
whyNot.2: X-linked recessive disorders affect mostly males, not both sexes equally.
whyNot.3: Y-linked traits pass father to son and never affect females.

reteach.title: Paint, stripes and a spare tire
reteach.question: Think of mixing paint, sewing a striped shirt, and driving a car with or without a spare tire. How do these match the non-Mendelian patterns?

blocks.body: Mixing red and white paint gives pink: incomplete dominance blends. Sewing red and white stripes side by side gives a shirt showing both colors: codominance shows both. Now the spare tire: a female has two X chromosomes, like a car with a spare, so one flat (a recessive allele) is covered. A male has one X and no spare, so a single flat stops the car: X-linked recessive traits show up in males.

blocks.text: Pink means blend (incomplete); AB or red-and-white hairs means both (codominant).

explain.body: Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is intermediate (pink snapdragons), and the F2 is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. Codominance: both alleles are fully expressed (AB blood, roan cattle).

test.q: Two pink snapdragons (RW x RW) are crossed. Which phenotype ratio is expected in the offspring?
test.why: RW x RW gives 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW; with incomplete dominance each genotype looks different, so 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

whyNot.0: This swaps the counts: the heterozygous pink class is the double one.
whyNot.1: 3:1 applies to complete dominance; here RW looks pink, not red.
whyNot.3: RR offspring are possible because both parents carry R.

explain.body: Three alleles in the population: IA, IB and i. IA and IB are codominant; both are dominant to i. Any one person still carries just two.

test.q: Which genotypes produce type A blood?
test.why: IA is dominant to i, so both IAIA and IAi give type A.

whyNot.0: IAIB is type AB, because IA and IB are codominant.

explain.body: X-linked genes: females XX (can be carriers), males XY (one copy shows). Fathers give X to daughters and Y to sons. Y-linked traits go father to son.

test.q: A trait controlled by a gene on the Y chromosome is passed from:
test.why: Only males have a Y chromosome, and fathers pass it to their sons.

whyNot.0: Mothers have no Y chromosome to pass on.
whyNot.2: Daughters receive their father's X, not his Y.
whyNot.3: Neither mothers nor daughters carry a Y chromosome.

explain.body: Pedigrees: squares male, circles female, shaded affected, half-shaded carrier. Recessive traits can skip generations. Autosomal recessive: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, Tay-Sachs, PKU. Autosomal dominant: Huntington, Marfan, achondroplasia.

test.q: Which disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern?
test.why: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant: one copy of the allele causes it.

whyNot.2: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive.
